3d • 

A few years ago, nobody asked me to find an AI Engineer. Now it's one of the most requested positions in the engineering space, and one of the most challenging to fill.

First, I had to figure out what I was looking for before I could source the right people. AI Engineer, AI Agent & Platform Engineer. These titles continue to morph with the ever-changing AI landscape, and haven't yet settled into a clear standard.

Finding talent is not the problem. LATAM has incredible engineers. The second goal was to create the missing framework around AI engineering positions.

The third flex is screening. To find the right talent for our clients, we have to know these roles inside and out. As engineering practices mature in the AI space, oftentimes the hard technical skills are not the only consideration. Soft skills such as curiosity and adaptability will tip the scales between equally qualified candidates.

The market is creating important new roles with no playbook. The exciting part of my job is to write them as I go.

I spent the past few years rebuilding security operations around LLMs, and the tooling kept dying under me: LangChain, then Dify, then OpenClaw. Everything now runs on Codex, Claude Code, and DeepSeek Harness, so I finally wrote down where I think this is going.
My answer: the next SOC looks like Codex. Engineers talk to agents in one workbench instead of working a ticket queue. A separate engine grinds through the alert volume around the clock. Humans keep exactly one job: approving high-risk actions. Three tiers of analysts collapse into one engineer supervising three tiers of agents.
The piece has the architecture, the four generations of tooling I burned through to get here, and the decoupling rules that keep you from getting locked into any one vendor. Tell me where I'm wrong.
